summary: Every Mandarin syllable has a tone — a pitch shape that is part of the word. There are four tones and a light neutral tone: mā (high and level), má (rising), mǎ (low, dipping), mà (falling), ma (short and light). Pinyin marks them over the main vowel. A few rules change tones in speech while the writing keeps the dictionary tone: a 3rd tone before another 3rd tone becomes a 2nd (你好 ní hǎo), 不 bù becomes bú before a 4th tone, and 一 yī becomes yí before a 4th tone and yì before the others.

blocks.title: Neutral tones
blocks.text: Particles (吗, 们, 了), the noun suffix 子 and the second syllable of many words have no tone of their own: xièxie 谢谢, péngyou 朋友, zhuōzi 桌子, xuésheng 学生.

blocks.title: Where the mark goes
blocks.text: On a or e if there is one (hǎo, xiè); in ou on the o (dōu); otherwise on the last vowel (duì, liù). The dot of i disappears under a mark: nǐ.

items.title: A language with stress, not tones
points: stress makes one syllable stronger and can tell words apart (German ÜBERsetzen ‘ferry across’ / überSETZen ‘translate’)

items.title: Chinese
points: every syllable has its own pitch shape
pitch changes the word itself: mǎi ‘buy’ ≠ mài ‘sell’
questions are made with 吗, not with the voice

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you say a word
questions: What tone does the dictionary give each syllable?
Is it a 3rd tone followed by another 3rd tone?
Is it 不 or 一 — and what tone follows?
Is the syllable a particle, a suffix or a repeated second syllable (toneless)?

askYourself: Which of the four tones (or neutral) does the dictionary give each syllable?
Is a 3rd tone followed by another 3rd tone? → say the first one as a 2nd tone (你好 ní hǎo).
Is a 3rd tone followed by any other tone? → only its low part (wǒ shì).
Is it 不 before a 4th tone? → bú (不是 bú shì); otherwise bù.
Is it 一 before a 4th tone → yí; before 1st, 2nd or 3rd → yì; counting, in a number or at the end → yī.
Is the syllable a particle (吗, 们), the suffix 子 or the second half of a word like 谢谢 or 朋友? → neutral, short and light.
Where does the mark go? a or e first, the o of ou, otherwise the last vowel.
steps: Learn every word with its dictionary tones.
Apply the sandhi rules when speaking; do not change the written pinyin of ordinary words.
Keep the tones in questions — add 吗 instead of raising the voice.

traps: Writing the sandhi tone in a dictionary search: look up nǐ hǎo, not ní hǎo.
Saying 不是 as bù shì — it is bú shì.
Saying 一个 as yī gè — it is yí ge.
Letting the voice rise at the end of a question: the last syllable keeps its own tone.
Giving full tones to toneless syllables: xièxie, not xièxiè.

quiz.q: How do you say 你好 (written nǐ hǎo)?
options: nǐ hǎo with two low tones
quiz.why: Two 3rd tones in a row: the first becomes a 2nd tone.
不 becomes bú before a 4th tone (shì).
个 is a 4th tone (gè) → 一 is said yí; 个 itself is usually light.
本 is a 3rd tone, so 一 becomes yì.
The grave accent ` marks the falling 4th tone (pitch 51).

quiz.q: Where does the tone mark go in hao?
quiz.why: a and e always take the mark when present.

quiz.q: What is the second syllable of 谢谢?
quiz.why: In a repeated word the second syllable is usually toneless.

quiz.q: In 很好 (hěn hǎo), which syllable changes?
quiz.why: The first of two 3rd tones becomes a 2nd tone.

notes.text: Greek has no tones: the accent mark shows stress, and stress can tell words apart (πότε ‘when’ / ποτέ ‘never’). In Chinese every syllable has its own pitch shape and there is no stress that tells words apart; toneless syllables (谢谢 xièxie) are simply short and light.

Russian stress is free and moves (го́род / города́), and pitch only colours the sentence — a question rises on the stressed word. In Chinese the pitch belongs to each syllable: mǎi 买 ‘buy’ / mài 卖 ‘sell’. A Russian-style questioning rise changes the tone, so ask with 吗 instead.

Spanish stress tells words apart (papa ‘potato’ / papá ‘dad’), pitch does not. Chinese has no such stress; instead the pitch of each syllable is fixed, so the habit of raising the voice on the last word of a question (¿Vienes?) has to give way to 吗.

English uses pitch for intonation (surprise, doubt, questions) and stress for words (REcord / reCORD) — a stress Chinese does not have. In Chinese the same pitch movements are parts of words: say 买 mǎi with a ‘questioning’ rise and it becomes another syllable. Ask with 吗 and keep every tone.

French has no lexical tones and only a light accent at the end of a phrase, so its even rhythm suits Chinese, where every syllable has a full beat. What is new is that each syllable needs one of four pitch shapes, and that only toneless particles (吗, 了) are short.

German has no tones: stress (ÜBERsetzen / überSETZen), vowel length (Staat / Stadt) and sentence melody carry meaning and emotion. Chinese has neither word stress nor vowel length, and an ‘annoyed’ falling voice on 妈 turns mā ‘mother’ into mà ‘to scold’ — feelings have to be shown with words and particles, not by bending the tone.

Hindi has no lexical tones (its neighbour Punjabi does); stress is light, and long and short vowels tell words apart (दिन ‘day’ / दीन ‘poor’), which Chinese never does. Every Chinese word has to be learned with its tones. Hindi’s aspirated / unaspirated pairs (प / फ) are a real help: Chinese b and p are exactly that contrast.

Persian has no tones and a predictable stress, mostly on the last syllable of a noun (ketā́b); pitch only shapes the sentence. In Chinese each syllable carries its own fixed pitch, so the tones are learned with every word.
Marathi has no lexical tones; pitch shows only the melody of the sentence. The four Chinese tones are new, and so is the neutral tone of particles and suffixes (吗, 了, 子), which are short and light.
Arabic tells words apart by consonants and vowel length (kataba / kātaba), never by pitch. Chinese does it by pitch: mā, má, mǎ, mà are four words — while vowel length tells nothing apart in Chinese.
Hebrew has no tones; stress, mostly on the last syllable, can tell words apart. In Chinese the pitch of every syllable tells words apart, and there is no word stress to learn.

Turkish has no tones; stress falls mostly on the last syllable and pitch only marks the sentence. Each Chinese syllable needs its own tone. Familiar: a yes/no question is made with a word (吗, like Turkish mı), not with the voice alone.

Japanese pitch accent already uses pitch to tell words apart (Tokyo hashi: 箸 ‘chopsticks’ high–low, 橋 ‘bridge’ low–high). Chinese goes further: every syllable has its own contour — level, rising, dipping or falling — not just high or low. Japanese long vowels (おばさん ‘aunt’ / おばあさん ‘grandmother’) have no Chinese counterpart: length never matters.

Standard Seoul Korean has no lexical tones (some south-eastern dialects have pitch accent). Chinese tones are new: learn each word with its pitch. Korean’s aspirated consonants (ㅍ, ㅌ, ㅋ) help with Chinese p, t, k.

Finnish tells words apart by length (tuli ‘fire’ / tuuli ‘wind’, kuka / kukka) and always stresses the first syllable. Chinese uses pitch instead, and length never matters; there is no fixed stress either.
Hungarian tells words apart by vowel length (kor ‘age’ / kór ‘disease’) and stresses the first syllable; pitch only marks the sentence. In Chinese length means nothing and pitch is part of each word.
Swahili, unlike most Bantu languages, has no tones, and its stress falls on the next-to-last syllable. In Chinese there is no stress rule; each syllable has its own pitch that must be learned.

Luganda is a tone language too: high and low pitches tell words apart and also mark grammar. Chinese tones are contours on every syllable (rising, dipping, falling) and they only tell words apart — they never mark tense or person. Luganda long vowels and consonants count; in Chinese length never does.

Vietnamese is tonal too (six tones in the north, all marked in the spelling: ma, má, mà, mả, mã, mạ). Chinese has fewer — four and a neutral one — but changes some of them in combination (sandhi: 你好 ní hǎo, 不是 bú shì), which the dictionary spelling does not show.
Inuktitut has no tones; it tells words apart by long and short vowels and consonants (written double, as in qujannamiik). In Chinese length never matters, but the pitch of every syllable does.

seeAlso.note: German has no tones: stress (ÜBERsetzen / überSETZen) and sentence intonation, not word pitch.
Arabic has no tones; what changes meaning is vowel length and the emphatic consonants.
Hebrew has no tones; stress, mostly on the last syllable, can tell words apart.
